\chapter{Fine Shades --- Four Differences a Translation Loses}
\label{ch:matices}
\hlchaptermodality{275}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can hear four Spanish distinctions that English translates identically, and say which of them no rule can teach me.}

Complete ES-C275-practice: say each pair and what English does with the difference.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[deber de]{deber de — one preposition, two entirely different claims}

\label{lesson:ES-C275-deber-de}



\begin{quote}
This chapter is about differences too small to be called mistakes and too large to ignore. The first one is a single word.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item deber — \textquotedblleft{}should, must\textquotedblright{}, which you already own.
  \item supongo que — the hedge that claims an inference.
\end{itemize}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{de-BER de}. The \emph{de} is unstressed and easy to miss, which is exactly the problem. $\to$ reference
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{deber} and \textbf{deber de} — and English uses one word, \emph{must}, for both.

\emph{Debe estar en casa.} — He \textbf{must} be at home. (Obligation: it is his duty.) \emph{Debe de estar en casa.} — He \textbf{must} be at home. (Inference: I conclude it.)

English hides this. \emph{He must be at home} is ambiguous in exactly the same way, and only context resolves it. Spanish has a marker available, and the marker is one unstressed syllable.

\emph{Deber} is Latin \textbf{debere}, \textquotedblleft{}to owe\textquotedblright{} — English \textbf{debt}, \textbf{debit}, \textbf{due}. The obligation sense is the original; the guessing sense is the borrowed one, which is why the plain form keeps it.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Two honest notes, because a rule stated too confidently here would mislead you.

First, this distinction is prescribed more consistently than it is observed. Many educated speakers use plain \emph{deber} for both, and the Real Academia accepts that while recommending the split. \textbf{You will hear it collapsed.} Knowing the distinction is for reading carefully and writing precisely, not for correcting anybody.

Second, it belongs beside \emph{supongo que}: both are ways of marking that a statement is reasoned rather than known. \emph{Deber de} puts that marking inside the verb.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item the obligation — \emph{debe estar en casa}
  \item the inference — \emph{debe de estar en casa}
  \item which one English cannot mark at all
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \emph{deber de} claim that \emph{deber} does not? (An inference rather than an obligation.) Is the distinction reliably observed in speech? (No — it is prescribed more than practised.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[cometer un error]{cometer un error — the verb the noun demands}

\label{lesson:ES-C275-cometer-un-error}



\begin{quote}
Nothing is wrong with the sentence you would build from first principles. It is simply not what anybody says.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item deber de — the modal shade.
  \item hacer — \textquotedblleft{}to do, to make\textquotedblright{}, the verb you would reach for.
\end{itemize}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{co-me-TER un e-RROR}. The double \emph{rr} is trilled. $\to$ reference
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{cometer un error} — \textquotedblleft{}to make a mistake.\textquotedblright{}

Not \emph{hacer un error}. That is grammatical, comprehensible, and wrong in the way that matters: no one says it. Spanish \textbf{commits} an error, as English commits a crime.

\emph{Cometer} is Latin \textbf{committere} — \emph{com-} (\textquotedblleft{}together\textquotedblright{}) plus \emph{mittere} (\textquotedblleft{}to send\textquotedblright{}), the root inside English \textbf{mission}, \textbf{transmit} and \textbf{commit}. English kept the verb for offences; Spanish extended it to mistakes.

The pairings are not deducible and have to be met one at a time: \emph{cometer un error}, \emph{tomar una decisión} (not \emph{hacer}), \emph{prestar atención} (to \emph{lend} attention), \emph{hacer una pregunta} (to \emph{make} a question, where English \emph{asks}).
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
A pairing of words that a language habitually uses together is a \textbf{collocation}, and it is the last thing to come right in a learner's output.

It is worth understanding why it feels so unfair. Grammar is a system you can learn, and vocabulary is a list you can study. Collocation is neither: it is \textbf{usage}, and the only source is having met the pair before.

This is why reading widely does something no amount of grammar study does, and why a sentence can be flawless and still sound foreign.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{cometer un error}
  \item the version you would have built, and why it is wrong (\emph{hacer} — no one says it)
  \item one more pair from the list above
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What is a collocation? (Words a language habitually uses together.) Why is it the last thing to come right? (It is usage — there is no rule to learn, only exposure.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[sí que]{sí que — the yes that answers an accusation nobody made}

\label{lesson:ES-C275-si-que}



\begin{quote}
English does this with the voice. Spanish does it with two words, and they leave a trace on the page.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item sí, claro — the ironic yes.
  \item cometer un error — the collocation.
\end{itemize}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{sí ke}, and the \emph{sí} keeps its accent because it is the affirming \emph{sí}, not the conditional \emph{si}. $\to$ reference
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{sí que} — the emphatic affirmative.

\emph{Habla español.} — He speaks Spanish. \emph{Sí que habla español.} — He \textbf{does} speak Spanish.

English marks this with stress alone — \emph{he DOES speak Spanish} — and in writing must resort to italics or the inserted \emph{do}. Spanish has a phrase for it, which means the emphasis \textbf{survives being written down}.

\emph{Sí} is Latin \textbf{sic}, \textquotedblleft{}thus, so\textquotedblright{} — the same \emph{sic} you meet in an English quotation meaning \emph{thus it stood}.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
What makes this a fine shade rather than a loud one is what it implies. \emph{Sí que habla español} does not simply assert. It \textbf{contradicts} — it answers a doubt, and if nobody voiced one, it invents one to answer.

That is a real risk in use: saying \emph{sí que} when no doubt existed tells your listener you thought they doubted you. Emphasis is never only volume; it always implies something about what the other person was thinking.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item the plain statement
  \item the emphatic one with \emph{sí que}
  \item what the emphatic version implies about your listener
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What Latin word is \emph{sí}? (\emph{Sic}, \textquotedblleft{}thus\textquotedblright{}.) What does \emph{sí que} do beyond asserting? (It contradicts a doubt — and implies one if none was voiced.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[delgado / flaco]{delgado / flaco — two words for one fact, and the choice is the message}

\label{lesson:ES-C275-delgado-flaco}



\begin{quote}
The last shade, and the one with consequences: two words that describe the same person and say different things about the speaker.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item sí que — the emphasis device.
  \item cansado — an adjective you already have.
\end{itemize}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{del-GA-do}, \emph{FLA-co}. $\to$ reference
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{delgado} and \textbf{flaco} both mean \textquotedblleft{}thin.\textquotedblright{}

\emph{Delgado} is Latin \textbf{delicatus} — the same word as English \textbf{delicate}. It is the neutral-to-complimentary one: slim.

\emph{Flaco} is Latin \textbf{flaccus}, \textquotedblleft{}flabby, drooping\textquotedblright{} — English \textbf{flaccid}. It is blunter, and depending on where you are and who you are talking to it ranges from plainly descriptive to unkind.

\textbf{Regional warning, and it matters more than the etymology.} In much of Latin America \emph{flaco} is affectionate — a common term of address to a friend, regardless of their build. In parts of Spain it lands harder. This is one of the places where a single word's warmth genuinely does not travel.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Two words with the same \textbf{denotation} — the fact they point at — and different \textbf{connotation} — what choosing one says about you.

This is where a dictionary stops being enough. It will give you both words and the same gloss for each, and the gloss is where the information you need has been removed.

That completes the four shades: a modal that marks a guess, a verb the noun insists on, an emphasis that implies a doubt, and a synonym that is not one. Every one of them is invisible to a translation and audible to a native speaker.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item both words
  \item which you would use about someone you had just met
  \item why a dictionary cannot tell you that
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What is the difference between denotation and connotation? (The fact a word points at; what choosing it says about you.) Which of the two thin-words travels worst between regions? (\emph{Flaco} — affectionate in much of Latin America, harder elsewhere.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[Practice]{Four differences a translation loses}

\label{lesson:ES-C275-practice}



\begin{quote}
Each of these four survives translation into English as the \emph{same sentence}. That is what makes them the last things you learn.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Your turn}
For each pair, say both and then say what English does with the difference.

Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{debe estar} and \emph{debe de estar} — English gives both \textbf{must}, and leaves you to guess which
  \item \emph{cometer un error} and the \emph{hacer} version — English cannot even see the error; both translate to \emph{make a mistake}
  \item \emph{habla español} and \emph{sí que habla español} — English needs the voice, or italics, and loses it in plain text
  \item \emph{delgado} and \emph{flaco} — English gives \textbf{thin} for both, and the dictionary removes exactly the information you needed
\end{itemize}

Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item which of the four could get you into trouble socially, and where (\emph{flaco} — warm in much of Latin America, harder elsewhere)
  \item which one no rule can teach you (the collocation — only having met it)
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Name the four: a guess marked in the verb, a verb the noun insists on, an emphasis that implies a doubt, and a synonym that is not one. What do all four have in common? (English translates them identically.)
\end{tcolorbox}
